summary: For ages 7–8, learners investigate that only some materials (iron, most steels, nickel, cobalt and many alloys containing them) are attracted to magnets — NOT all metals and NOT all shiny things — through a predict-test-record-conclude cycle with deliberately chosen counter-examples, including shiny non-ferrous metals so shininess and metal-ness are held constant. A second strand gives first-hand experience of both attraction AND repulsion between two magnets, and separates 'attracted to a magnet' from 'being a magnet' via a flip-test. The goal is an empirical, testable property discovered by hands-on investigation, not any model of fields or domains (reserve that for later).
misconceptions: 'All metals are magnetic / magnets stick to any metal' — THE robust misconception, reinforced by earlier conductor/insulator (metals-are-special) teaching, and frequently held by teachers themselves (IOP Spark; NSTA).
'Anything shiny or silver-coloured is magnetic' — the same error generalised by appearance rather than material.
Confusing 'attracted to a magnet' with 'is a magnet'.
'Bigger magnet = stronger magnet' — strength depends on material, not just size (IOP Spark).
Merging magnetism with static electricity or with gravity (both act at a distance, so children conflate them).

activities.title: Predict–test–record–conclude with a confound-rich object set
steps: Lay out a mixed set of everyday objects chosen to break the rule: a steel paperclip and steel scissors (attract), beside a solid copper item (e.g. a short piece of copper pipe or wire), an aluminium can-ring/tab, a solid brass key, a plastic brick and a wooden block (don't). The adult should check each item with a magnet beforehand: many 'copper' coins (e.g. UK 1p/2p from 1992 onwards, euro 1–5 cent coins) are copper-plated steel and DO stick, and some keys are steel.
Before testing, predict for EACH object whether a magnet will stick to it, and say WHY.

Include three SHINY items together — a shiny steel paperclip, a shiny solid copper item (pre-checked; not a copper-plated steel coin) and a shiny aluminium tab — so that all three are shiny and all are metal, and the difference that matters is the material they are made of.
Bring a magnet to each object in turn and observe whether it is attracted or not.
Record each result in two columns: magnetic vs non-magnetic.
Look at the magnetic column and conclude what those objects have in common — they are iron/steel (and, when named, nickel/cobalt).
Repeat with a dull, rusty iron nail alongside a shiny solid copper item (pre-checked as non-magnetic) to check whether shininess predicts attraction.
activities.insight: Magnets attract specific materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), not metals-in-general and not shiny/silver-coloured things. The deciding factor is what the material actually is, not whether it is a metal or whether it looks shiny.

activities.title: Feel both attraction and repulsion between two magnets
steps: Bring two bar magnets together one way and feel them snap together (attract).
Flip one magnet end-for-end and bring the SAME two magnets together again — feel them push apart (repel), including the invisible 'push' before they touch.
Repeat the attract-then-flip-to-repel test several times so the response is felt as a stable, repeatable property.
Describe in your own words that two magnets can BOTH attract and repel depending on which ends face each other.
activities.insight: Attraction and repulsion are two faces of one magnetic force between magnets; a magnet can push as well as pull, and which happens depends on which poles face each other (orientation), not chance.

activities.title: Flip-test: 'attracted to a magnet' vs 'is a magnet'
steps: Stick a paperclip to a magnet and notice it is attracted.
Ask: is the paperclip itself now a magnet? Decide how to check.
Turn the magnet around (so the opposite pole faces the paperclip) and bring it to the paperclip again — observe that the paperclip is still attracted, never repelled.
Contrast with a known second magnet, which IS repelled when a like pole is turned toward it.
Conclude that something attracted to a magnet is a magnetic material, but a true magnet is the thing that can also repel when turned around.
activities.insight: Being attracted to a magnet (a magnetic material) is not the same as being a magnet. The distinguishing test is repulsion: a magnetic material is attracted whichever way the magnet faces, while only another magnet can be made to push away when a like pole is turned toward it.

activities.title: Keep magnetism distinct from static electricity and gravity
steps: Rub a balloon to charge it and see it attract small bits of paper or hair; compare this with how a magnet behaves toward the sorted objects.

Discuss that although both a charged balloon and a magnet can act without touching, a magnet only attracts iron/steel-type materials while the charged balloon attracts light bits of many different materials.
State that magnetism is a property of certain materials, separate from gravity, which pulls everything down regardless of material.
activities.insight: Magnetism, static electricity and gravity are different forces; acting at a distance is something they share, but they are not the same thing and should not be merged.

checkQuestion: I have a shiny copper coin, a shiny steel paperclip, and a shiny aluminium can-tab. I hold a magnet near each one. Which will the magnet pull and which won't — and what makes the difference between them?
checkAnswer: Only the steel paperclip is pulled. Magnets attract iron and steel (and nickel and cobalt), not other metals like copper or aluminium — so it isn't shininess or 'being a metal' that matters, but what the material actually is.
